questions.title: Risks and prevention
questions.text: Match each physical risk to the best prevention.

questions.title: UPS
questions.text: Explain how a UPS protects data when the mains power fails.

scheme.mark_scheme: Battery supplies power for a short time after the mains fails (1); so data can be saved and the computer shut down safely / files not corrupted (1)
scheme.model_answer: Its battery keeps the computer running for a few minutes, giving time to save the work and shut down safely so files are not corrupted.

questions.title: Human error
questions.text: State **two** ways to reduce data loss caused by human error.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): staff training; access rights / read-only files; regular backups; recycle bin / undo; confirmation messages before deleting
scheme.model_answer:
1 Make regular backups so deleted files can be restored.
2 Give staff read-only access to files they should not change.

scheme.mark_scheme: A copy of data made at regular intervals (1) stored separately so it can be restored if the original is lost (1)
scheme.model_answer: A copy of data made regularly and kept separately, so that it can be restored if the original data is lost.

questions.title: Types of backup
questions.text: Match each type of backup to its description.

right.text: Copies all the data every time
Copies only data changed since the last backup of any kind
Copies all data changed since the last full backup

questions.title: Restoring backups
questions.text: A full backup is made on Sunday and **incremental** backups on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday. The disk fails on Thursday. Which backups are needed to restore the data?

options.content: Sunday's full backup and Wednesday's backup
Sunday's full backup and the Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday backups

scheme.mark_scheme: C

questions.title: 3-2-1 rule
questions.text: The 3-2-1 backup rule: keep [[1]] copies of the data, on [[2]] different types of media, with [[3]] copy stored off-site.

questions.title: Fire
questions.text: A company wants to be sure its data survives a fire.

fields.label: Describe how backup helps prevent data loss in the event of a fire
Suggest one recommendation so that the latest data is not lost

scheme.mark_scheme: How: if the original is destroyed, the backup can be used to restore it / cloud copy on remote servers not affected by the fire (1). Recommendation: back up after every critical change / store a copy in a location separate from the fire area (1)
scheme.model_answer:
How: the data destroyed in the fire can be restored from the backup.
Recommendation: make backups after every important change and keep them in a different building or the cloud.

questions.title: Backup media
questions.text: Give **one** advantage of each backup medium.

scheme.mark_scheme: Cloud: off-site / automatic / accessible anywhere (1). External HDD: cheap / large / fast / no Internet needed (1). Tape: very large capacity / cheap per GB / long life (1)
scheme.model_answer:
| Medium | Advantage |
|---|---|
| Cloud | Stored off-site, so safe from a fire in the building |
| External HDD | Cheap and fast for large amounts of data |
| Tape | Huge capacity at low cost |

questions.title: Disk mirroring
questions.text: Describe how disk mirroring protects data.

scheme.mark_scheme: Data is written to two disks at the same time / identical copies in real time (1); if one disk fails the other continues without interruption / no data lost (1)
scheme.model_answer: Every change is written to two disks at the same time, so if one disk fails the system carries on using the identical second disk.

questions.title: Mirroring advantage
questions.text: Describe **one** advantage of disk mirroring over backup.

scheme.mark_scheme: Instant data recovery in case of one disk failure / work continues without interruption / real-time data synchronised so nothing is lost (1)
scheme.model_answer: If one disk fails, the system keeps working immediately with up-to-date data on the second disk.

questions.title: Mirroring and viruses
questions.text: Disk mirroring protects data against ransomware, because a clean copy is kept on the second disk.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: The encrypted (or deleted) data is copied to the second disk immediately.

questions.title: Backup vs mirroring
questions.text: Tick (✓) the method each statement describes.

prefill: Data is copied continuously in real time
Older versions of a file can be restored
Can be stored off-site to survive a fire
The system continues with no downtime if a disk fails

scheme.mark_scheme: Mirroring; backup; backup; mirroring (1 each)

questions.title: Consequences
questions.text: The absence or improper implementation of data protection measures may lead to negative consequences. Give **one** consequence for each measure. Do not repeat your answers.

scheme.mark_scheme: Backup: data loss / losing critical data after hardware failure, human error or malicious activity (1). Mirroring: downtime while data is recovered / operational disruption / storage capacity reduced / a failed drive left unreplaced (1). Do not accept repeated answers.
scheme.model_answer:
Data backup: critical data is lost for ever after a disk failure.
Disk mirroring: the system stops (downtime) while the data is recovered.

questions.title: Use both
questions.text: Explain why a bank uses **both** disk mirroring and backups.

scheme.mark_scheme: Mirroring keeps the system running with no data loss if a disk fails (1); backups (off-site, older versions) protect against deletion, ransomware, fire or theft, which mirroring cannot (1)
scheme.model_answer: Mirroring keeps transactions running without loss if a disk breaks, but it copies mistakes and is in the same building; off-site backups let the bank restore older versions after ransomware, deletion or fire.

questions.title: Risks in a company
questions.text: A small company keeps all its customer and order data on one server in its office.

parts.title: Risks
parts.text: Describe **two** physical risks to the data and one way to prevent each.

scheme.mark_scheme: Each risk (1) + matching prevention (1): hardware failure – mirroring / backup; power cut – UPS; fire / flood – off-site backup / fire detection; theft – locks / CCTV / encryption; overheating – air conditioning; human error – training / access rights
scheme.model_answer:
1 A power cut could corrupt files while they are being saved — install a UPS.
2 A fire could destroy the server — keep backups in the cloud.

parts.title: Location
parts.text: The company backs up to an external disk kept next to the server. Explain why this is not enough.

scheme.mark_scheme: A fire / flood / theft in the office would destroy or remove both the server and the backup (1); the backup should be kept off-site / in the cloud (1)
scheme.model_answer: A fire or theft would affect the server and the disk together, so the data would be lost; one copy should be kept off-site or in the cloud.

parts.title: UPS
parts.text: Explain why the company should connect the server to a UPS.

scheme.mark_scheme: Battery keeps the server running during a power cut (1); data can be saved / server shut down safely, avoiding corruption (1)
scheme.model_answer: During a power cut the UPS battery keeps the server on long enough to save data and shut down safely.

questions.title: Backups
questions.text: The company decides to make a **full** backup every Sunday and **differential** backups on the other days.

scheme.mark_scheme: Copies all data changed (1) since the last full backup (1)
scheme.model_answer: It copies every file that has changed since the last full backup.

parts.title: Restore
parts.text: The server fails on Thursday morning. State which backups are needed to restore the data and what data will still be lost.

scheme.mark_scheme: Sunday's full backup + Wednesday's differential (1); changes made on Thursday before the failure are lost (1)
scheme.model_answer: Sunday's full backup and Wednesday's differential; the changes made on Thursday before the crash are lost.

parts.title: Compare
parts.text: Compare differential backups with incremental backups.

scheme.mark_scheme: Incremental copies changes since the last backup of any kind, so each is smaller / faster (1); but restoring needs every incremental, whereas differential needs only the full + latest differential (1)
scheme.model_answer: Incremental backups are smaller and faster because they copy only changes since the last backup, but restoring needs all of them; a differential is bigger but only the latest one is needed with the full backup.

parts.title: Good practice
parts.text: Explain why the company should regularly test restoring its backups.

scheme.mark_scheme: A backup may be incomplete / corrupted / unreadable (1); testing ensures the data can actually be recovered when needed (1)
scheme.model_answer: Backups can be corrupted or incomplete; testing a restore proves the data can really be recovered in an emergency.

questions.title: Disk mirroring
questions.text: The company's online shop must work 24 hours a day, so the server uses disk mirroring.

scheme.mark_scheme: Data written to two disks at the same time (1); the disks are identical, so if one fails the other is used (1)
scheme.model_answer: Each piece of data is written to two disks at once, so they are identical; if one disk fails the other takes over.

parts.title: Advantage
parts.text: Explain **one** advantage of disk mirroring over backup for the online shop.

scheme.mark_scheme: Instant recovery / no downtime when a disk fails (1); the shop keeps taking orders with no data lost (1)
scheme.model_answer: If a disk fails the shop keeps running immediately with all the latest orders, so no sales are lost.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): copies deletions / viruses / ransomware; no protection against fire / theft (same place); halves storage capacity / extra cost; controller failure affects both
scheme.model_answer:
1 Deleted or encrypted files are copied to the mirror too.
2 Both disks are destroyed together in a fire.

parts.title: Consequence
parts.text: Explain the consequence of not replacing a failed mirrored disk quickly.

scheme.mark_scheme: The system runs on a single disk with no copy (1); if that disk also fails, all data is lost / downtime (1)
scheme.model_answer: The server then has only one disk with no mirror, so if that disk fails too all the data is lost and the shop stops.

summary: Physical and environmental risks that cause data loss (hardware failure, power problems, fire, flood, theft, accidental damage, human error) and how to prevent them; backups — full, incremental and differential, media, the 3-2-1 rule, schedules and off-site storage; disk mirroring (RAID 1) and other RAID levels; a detailed comparison of backup and mirroring, and the consequences of not using them.

blocks.content: Data can be lost not only through hackers and viruses but also through **physical** events that damage or destroy the **hardware** where it is stored. These are **physical risks**.

blocks.title: Physical risks and how to prevent them
rows: Hard disk crash, overheating, worn-out SSD, failed power supply
Backups, RAID mirroring, cooling, replacing old hardware, monitoring disk health
Data in RAM lost; files corrupted while being saved
**Off-site / cloud backups**, fire-proof safes, smoke detectors and gas fire suppression, servers above ground level
Laptop, server or USB drive stolen
Locks, CCTV, security staff, alarm systems, **encryption** of portable devices
Coffee spilt on a laptop, device dropped
Deleting or overwriting files, formatting the wrong disk
Training, access rights, backups, "recycle bin", confirmation messages
Someone plugs a USB into a server
Locked server rooms, ID cards, **biometric** doors, visitor logs

items.title: Environmental risks
items.content:
- **Heat** — computers overheat and fail; server rooms need **air conditioning**.
- **Humidity and water** — corrosion and short circuits; keep away from pipes and windows.
- **Dust** — blocks fans and causes overheating; regular cleaning.
- **Magnetic fields** — can damage data on magnetic disks and tapes.

items.title: Effects of losing data
items.content:
- Work must be **redone**; orders, records and history may be **lost for ever**.
- The organisation may **stop working** (downtime) and lose **money** and **customers**.
- Personal data on a stolen device can lead to **identity theft** and **legal** consequences.

blocks.title: UPS — uninterruptible power supply
blocks.content: A **battery unit** between the mains and the computer. When the power fails it supplies electricity for a few minutes, so the computer can **save the data** and **shut down safely**. It also protects against **surges** and **spikes**.
A **copy of data** made at regular times and stored **separately** (another disk, tape, cloud, another building) so that the data can be **restored** after loss.

items.title: Full backup
items.content: Copies **all** data every time. Easy to restore; slow and uses most storage.

items.title: Incremental backup
items.content: Copies only data **changed since the last backup** (of any kind). Fast, small; restoring needs the full backup plus every increment.

items.title: Differential backup
items.content: Copies everything changed **since the last full backup**. Restoring needs only the full backup and the latest differential.

blocks.title: Restoring after a crash on Thursday
blocks.content:
A full backup is made on **Sunday**; the disk fails on **Thursday morning**.
| Strategy | Backups made | What is needed to restore |
|---|---|---|
| Full every day | Full Sun, Mon, Tue, Wed | Only **Wednesday's** full backup |
| Full + incremental | Full Sun; incremental Mon, Tue, Wed | Sunday full **+ Mon + Tue + Wed** incrementals (in order) |
| Full + differential | Full Sun; differential Mon, Tue, Wed | Sunday full **+ Wednesday's** differential |

In every case the work done **on Thursday before the crash** is lost — it was not yet backed up.

blocks.title: Backup media and locations
rows: Can be lost, stolen or damaged with the computer if kept nearby
In the same building — fire or theft affects both
Needs Internet; monthly cost; data held by a third party (security)
Very large and cheap per GB, long life

items.title: Good backup practice
items.content:
- **Regular schedule** — daily, or after every **critical change**; automatic where possible.
- **3-2-1 rule** — keep **3** copies of the data, on **2** different media, with **1** copy **off-site** (another building or the cloud).
- Store backups **in a location separate from the original** — so a fire or flood does not destroy both.
- **Encrypt** backups and keep them **secure**.
- **Test** restoring regularly — a backup that cannot be restored is useless.
- Keep **several older versions** (e.g. grandfather–father–son rotation) to recover from viruses or mistakes found later.

blocks.content: Data is written to **two (or more) disks at the same time**, so the disks are identical copies. If one disk fails, the system continues using the other **without interruption**.

write "Order 1052"
   Computer ─────────┬─────────────
                     │             │
                ┌────▼────┐   ┌────▼────┐
                │ Disk 1  │   │ Disk 2  │     identical copies
                │ Order…  │   │ Order…  │
                └─────────┘   └─────────┘
   Disk 1 fails → the system keeps running from Disk 2; the failed disk is replaced
   and the mirror is rebuilt.
blocks.caption: Disk mirroring: every write goes to both disks

items.title: Advantages of mirroring
items.content:
- **Instant data recovery** if one disk fails — no restore needed.
- The system keeps **working without interruption** — business continuity.
- **No data is lost** — every change is on both disks in **real time**.
- Reading can be faster (data read from either disk).

items.title: Disadvantages of mirroring
items.content:
- **Storage capacity is halved** — two disks hold one copy of data; extra cost.
- Copies **mistakes** too: deleted files, viruses and ransomware are written to both disks immediately.
- Both disks are in the **same place** — no protection against fire, flood or theft.
- If the **controller** fails, both disks may be affected; a failed disk must be replaced quickly.

blocks.title: RAID levels (Redundant Array of Independent Disks)
rows: Data split across disks for speed
Data and parity spread over 3+ disks
**Yes** — survives one disk failure; uses less extra space than mirroring

blocks.title: Backup vs disk mirroring
rows: Usually in the **same** computer or server
Yes, but data since the last backup is **lost** and restoring takes **time**
**No** — the deletion or corruption is copied to the mirror immediately
Needs a second identical disk for every disk

blocks.content: The key comparison: **mirroring gives continuous availability** but copies mistakes too; a **backup can restore earlier versions** but is only as recent as the last backup. Organisations usually use **both**.

blocks.title: Consequences of not using these measures
rows: **Data loss** — critical data lost for ever after hardware failure, human error, fire or malware; work must be redone
**Downtime** while data is recovered or reconstructed; **operational disruption**; transactions lost since the last backup
Storage capacity reduced by the copies; a failed drive left unreplaced means the next failure loses data
Fire, flood or theft destroys the original and the backup together

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Describe how backup helps prevent data loss in the event of a fire. [1]**
If the original data is destroyed in the fire, the **backup** (stored elsewhere / in the cloud) can be used to **restore** it (1).

**Q: Suggest one recommendation to ensure that the latest data is not lost in the event of a fire. [1]**
Perform backups **after every critical change** / store a copy **in a location separate from the fire area** (1).

**Q: Describe one advantage of disk mirroring over backup. [1]**
**Instant recovery** — if one disk fails the system **continues without interruption** with up-to-date data on the second disk (1).

**Q: Give one consequence of not using data backup. [1]**
**Loss of critical data** after hardware failure, human error or malware (1).

- Saying mirroring protects against **viruses** or **deletion** — it **copies** them to the second disk.
- Saying a backup is "a second disk that is always up to date" — that is **mirroring**.
- Keeping backups in the **same room** as the original and claiming they protect against fire.
- Confusing **incremental** (since the last backup) and **differential** (since the last full backup).
